tool.name: SplitLinesIntoSegments
tool.summary: Converts each polyline into a new PolylineZ feature class with one true three-dimensional feature per straight segment, carrying optional per-segment topography attributes (coordinates, lengths, slope, bearing, deflection/inclination/3D-deflection angles, and more) and any chosen fields copied from the source table. The output displays in space in a Scene and is symbolized with Unclassed Colors.
tool.usage:
This is the companion to Topography along Lines. Instead of summarizing the topography of each whole line into fields on that line, it breaks every line into its individual straight segments and writes each segment as its own three-dimensional feature, so you can compute your own statistics on subsets of segments, or symbolize the segments by slope, direction, or any other value.
Segmentation and elevation source. Each line is reduced to straight segments exactly as in Topography along Lines: from the polylines' own Z values (each existing vertex becomes a segment end), or by sampling a DEM by bilinear interpolation at a regular ground interval equal to the smaller of the DEM's cell width and height. The original vertices are always kept, so real bends fall on segment ends (not rounded across samples). Sample points are projected into the DEM's coordinate system for sampling (the DEM itself is never projected); the output features are written in the source polylines' coordinate system with Z from the sampled elevation, so they are true PolylineZ features that draw in space in a Scene. Multipart lines are handled part by part, with no segment bridging disconnected pieces.
Direction of travel. The angle fields (deflection, inclination, 3D deflection) and the signed fields (relative elevation change, relative slope) describe each segment relative to the one before it, in the direction of the line's geometry (first vertex to last). The three angle fields need a preceding segment, so the first segment of each line or part has no value for them: null in a geodatabase, or -999 in a shapefile (which cannot store null).
Segment attributes (the Property list): • Coordinates (in the dataset's coordinate system): Begin X/Y/Z, End X/Y/Z, Midpoint X/Y/Z. • Lengths: Planimetric Length (geodesic, X/Y only), Surface Length (geodesic, the true 3-D length), Surface Ratio (surface / planimetric). • Elevation: Relative Elevation Change (signed: + uphill, - downhill), Net Elevation Change (its absolute value), Mean Elevation. • Slope: Relative Slope (signed) and Absolute Slope (positive), in the chosen slope unit. • Bearing: the segment's compass azimuth (0-360, from north). • Turn angles relative to the previous segment: Deflection Angle (horizontal, the change in bearing; signed) and Absolute Deflection Angle; Inclination Angle (vertical, the change in slope/pitch; signed) and Absolute Inclination Angle; 3D Deflection Angle (the full three-dimensional angle between the previous and current segment; always positive). • Identity: Source Line ID (the parent polyline's ObjectID, for grouping segments back to their line), Segment Number (order within the part), Part Index, Slope Direction Class ("Uphill"/"Downhill"/"Flat"), and Station (cumulative distance along the line at the segment's start).
Choosing fields. In the Segment Attributes list, use the Property column's drop-down to check off as many attributes as you like; each new row's output field name is filled in automatically (prefixed "Seg_", e.g. Seg_Surface_Length) so it never clashes with a field created by Topography along Lines or with a copied source field. When the output will be a shapefile, whose field names are limited to 10 characters, short names such as SgSurfLen are filled in instead, and the names are swapped if you change the output to the other kind of dataset. You can edit any name. Fields are created with the right type (double, long integer, or text).
Copying source fields. Use the "Source fields to copy" drop-down to check off any fields from the input table to carry onto every segment of each line. Copied fields keep their type and name where possible; a name that would be invalid, reserved (like Shape_Length), or a duplicate is adjusted automatically.
Units. Coordinates are in the dataset's coordinate system units; lengths and station in the chosen Length Unit; elevation change and elevation in the DEM's or polylines' elevation units; slopes (relative and absolute) in the chosen Slope Unit (degrees or percent); all angles and bearings in degrees. Slopes are computed internally in degrees and converted for reporting.
Symbology. When the output is added to the map it is symbolized with Unclassed Colors on a blue-to-yellow-to-red ramp, using the highest-priority attribute you calculated in this order: Mean Elevation, Begin X, End X, Absolute Slope, Relative Slope; if none of those were calculated, the first attribute you chose is used.
References: surface length follows the three-dimensional distance concept of Jenness, J. S. 2004 (Calculating landscape surface area from digital elevation models, Wildlife Society Bulletin 32:829-839); the remaining fields (coordinates, lengths, slopes, bearings, and inter-segment turn angles) are elementary geometry.

dialogReference.para: The polyline feature class to split into segment features. If a selection is active, only the selected features are processed.

The new feature class to create: one true PolylineZ feature per straight segment, in the input's coordinate system. A suggested name is filled in from the input. Save to a geodatabase to allow null values in the first-segment angle fields (a shapefile stores -999 instead).
Where elevations come from. Z values from the polylines uses the lines' own vertex Z (Z-enabled input only). DEM raster samples a DEM. Set to DEM automatically when the input is not Z-enabled.

The DEM to sample (used when the Elevation source is DEM). Sample points are placed at the smaller of the cell width and height, projected into the DEM's coordinate system, and interpolated bilinearly.
The elevation units (Meters or Feet) of the DEM or the polylines' Z. Filled in and locked when the vertical coordinate system defines them; you are asked only when they are undefined.

Each row pairs a Property (segment attribute) with the output field it is written to. Use the Property drop-down to check off several at once; the field names auto-fill (prefixed "Seg_") and can be edited. See the tool description for each property's meaning and units. Optional -- with none chosen the tool still creates the bare segment features.

Fields from the input table to copy onto every segment. Use the drop-down to check off several at once. Copied fields keep their type and name where legal; invalid, reserved, or duplicate names are adjusted automatically.
The unit for the length and station fields: Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles, Yards, or Nautical Miles. Coordinates use the dataset's units; elevation fields use the elevation units.
The unit for the Relative Slope and Absolute Slope fields: Degrees or Percent. Used only when a slope attribute is selected.

scriptExample.title: Split Lines into Topography Segments example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Create a 3-D segment feature class from a DEM, choosing a few attributes and copying a source field. surface_attributes is a list of [property, field] pairs (property first); copy_fields is a list of [field] rows. Valid Property strings are exactly: "Begin X", "Begin Y", "Begin Z", "End X", "End Y", "End Z", "Planimetric Length (geodesic)", "Surface Length (geodesic)", "Surface Ratio", "Relative Elevation Change", "Net Elevation Change", "Relative Slope", "Absolute Slope", "Bearing", "Deflection Angle", "Absolute Deflection Angle", "Inclination Angle", "Absolute Inclination Angle", "3D Deflection Angle", "Source Line ID", "Segment Number", "Part Index", "Slope Direction Class", "Station (distance along line)", "Midpoint X", "Midpoint Y", "Midpoint Z", "Mean Elevation". elev_source: "DEM raster" or "Z values from the polylines". length_unit: "Meters", "Kilometers", "Feet", "Miles", "Yards", "Nautical Miles". slope_unit: "Degrees", "Percent".
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.SplitLinesIntoSegments( in_lines=r"C:\Project\Trails.gdb\trails", out_fc=r"C:\Project\Trails.gdb\trail_segments", elev_source="DEM raster", in_dem=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM", elev_units="Meters", surface_attributes=[ ["Mean Elevation", "Seg_Mean_Elevation"], ["Surface Length (geodesic)", "Seg_Surface_Length"], ["Absolute Slope", "Seg_Absolute_Slope"], ["Bearing", "Seg_Bearing"], ["3D Deflection Angle", "Seg_3D_Deflection_Angle"], ["Source Line ID", "Seg_Source_ID"]], copy_fields=[["TrailName"], ["Trail_Class"]], length_unit="Meters", slope_unit="Degrees")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Converts polylines into a PolylineZ feature class of individual 3-D segments with optional per-segment topography attributes (coordinates, lengths, slope, bearing, deflection/inclination/3D-deflection angles, source line ID, and more) and copied source fields; geodesic, real 3-D for Scene display, symbolized with Unclassed Colors.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Companion to Topography along Lines. Reduces each polyline to straight segments (from the polylines' own Z or a DEM sampled by bilinear interpolation, keeping original vertices) and writes each segment as a true PolylineZ feature in the source coordinate system, so the output draws in space in a Scene. Optional per-segment fields include start/end/midpoint coordinates, planimetric and surface length, surface ratio, relative and net elevation change, relative and absolute slope, bearing, deflection and inclination and 3D-deflection angles (relative to the previous segment; null or -999 on the first segment of each part), source line ID, segment number, part index, slope-direction class, station, and mean elevation. Any source fields can be copied onto the segments (names adjusted to avoid reserved/duplicate names). Output is symbolized with Unclassed Colors on a blue-to-yellow-to-red ramp by the highest-priority attribute calculated. Surface length follows Jenness, J. S. 2004, Wildlife Society Bulletin 32:829-839.
dataIdInfo.idCredit: Tool by Jeff Jenness, Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com). Surface length: Jenness, J. S. 2004. Calculating landscape surface area from digital elevation models. Wildlife Society Bulletin 32:829-839. Suggested citation: Jenness, J. (2026). Split Lines into Topography Segments. Jenness Enterprises Wildlife and Forestry Tools for ArcGIS Pro. Available at: http://www.jennessent.com.
